    Section 1

    What respect at work looks like

    Most of us know when something feels off. The harder part can be knowing when a line has been crossed and what to do next.

    At Vista, the expectation is straightforward: treat people with respect. That applies in the office, in a field truck, on a construction site, at a client location, in camp, and anywhere else work takes us. If something happens, speak up. Reports are taken seriously, investigated, and workers who raise concerns in good faith are protected from retaliation.

    Where the law draws the line

    Most people have an idea of what counts as violence or harassment. The definitions in Alberta's Occupational Health and Safety Act are more specific, and they are the ones that apply on our sites.

    Definitions

    Work site

    A location where a worker is, or is likely to be, engaged in any occupation, and includes any vehicle or mobile equipment used by a worker in an occupation.

    Workplace violence

    Whether at a work site or work-related, means the threatened, attempted or actual conduct of a person that causes or is likely to cause physical or psychological injury or harm, and includes domestic or sexual violence.

    Harassment

    Means any single incident or repeated incidents of objectionable or unwelcome conduct, comment, bullying or action by a person that the person knows or ought reasonably to know will or would cause offence or humiliation to a worker, or adversely affects the worker's health and safety, and includes conduct, comment, bullying or action because of race, religious beliefs, colour, physical disability, mental disability, age, ancestry, place of origin, marital status, source of income, family status, gender, gender identity, gender expression and sexual orientation, and a sexual solicitation or advance, but excludes any reasonable conduct of an employer or supervisor in respect of the management of workers or a work site.

    Three things worth noticing in those definitions.
    • A crew truck, a client's office, a remote line-cutting site and a camp room are all work sites.
    • Harassment can be a single incident. It does not have to be repeated to count.
    • The test is not what you meant. It is what you knew, or ought reasonably to have known, the effect would be.

    Not every difficult conversation is harassment

    Reasonable management of workers and the work site is excluded from the definition. Assigning work, setting schedules, evaluating performance, inspecting sites, enforcing safety rules and applying discipline with just cause are not harassment when they are done reasonably and fairly. A difference of opinion or a minor disagreement between co-workers is not harassment either.

    A supervisor gives an employee respectful, specific feedback about repeated errors and explains what needs to improve. The employee is upset by the conversation. Does that automatically make it harassment?

    Correct. Supervisors can assign work, address performance and enforce expectations when it is done reasonably and respectfully. Harassment is not the same as a difficult or uncomfortable workplace conversation.

    Not quite. A worker can be uncomfortable with feedback without the conversation being harassment. Reasonable, respectful management of work and performance is excluded from the definition.

    Section 2

    Responsibilities

    A respectful workplace is not something HR or HSE can create on their own. Everyone has a part in it.

    What we say, what we do, and what we choose to ignore all shape the workplace. Vista has responsibilities as an employer, supervisors have responsibilities to the people they lead, and every worker is responsible for their own conduct and for speaking up when something is not right.

    Obligations of work site parties

    Employers, supervisors and workers each have specific duties they must follow to address harassment and violence at the workplace.

    • Employers must ensure workers are not subject to, or participate in, harassment or violence at the work site.
    • Supervisors must ensure workers under their supervision are not subject to harassment or violence at the work site.
    • Workers must refrain from causing or participating in harassment or violence.

    Section 3

    Would you recognize it in the moment?

    Harassment does not always look dramatic. It can be a comment, a pattern, a threat, unwanted attention, or behaviour that slowly makes someone dread coming to work.

    People often picture harassment as something obvious. In real life, it can be harder to label, especially when it comes from someone you work with every day, someone senior to you, or a client. Understanding the behaviours makes it easier to recognize when normal workplace friction has crossed into something unacceptable.

    Five cumulative aspects of harassment

    Where a complaint is assessed, these five aspects are generally considered together.

    1. Vexatious behaviourConduct that is humiliating, offensive or abusive to the person on the receiving end.
    2. In the form of repeated conduct, verbal comments, actions or gesturesA single serious incident can also meet the definition on its own.
    3. That is hostile or unwantedThe behaviour is unwelcome to the person it is aimed at.
    4. That affects the employee's dignity, or psychological or physical integrityThe impact lands on the person, not just the task.
    5. That makes the work environment harmfulThe cumulative effect is a workplace that is no longer safe or healthy.

    The forms you could encounter

    Select a type to read what it looks like in practice. Two of them open into further tabs.

    A crew chief tells a new hire that overtime on the good jobs "depends on how friendly you decide to be" and puts a hand on their back. Which two labels fit best?

    Correct. A job benefit is being offered in exchange for sexual or romantic conduct, and the crew chief is using a position of authority over a subordinate. Unwanted touching is also physical in nature.

    Have another look. A job benefit is being tied to "friendliness", that is quid pro quo sexual harassment, and it is being done by someone with authority over the worker, which is power harassment.

    Section 4

    When behaviour starts to escalate

    Serious incidents can be preceded by warning signs. Recognizing escalation early gives you more options to protect yourself and others.

    You are not expected to diagnose someone or put yourself in danger. The goal is to notice concerning behaviour, avoid escalating it, get to safety when needed, and report it early. Open each stage for practical guidance.

    Your safety comes first. Nothing in this course expects you to stay in a situation that has become threatening. Leave, get to a safe place, call 911 if there is immediate danger, and report as soon as you are safe.

    Effects of harassment and violence

    The damage does not stop when the incident does. It shows up in three places.

    Section 5

    What to do when something happens

    If it happens to you, or you see it happening

    1. Address the harassmentIf it is safe to do so, tell the person that their behaviour is unwelcome and ask them to stop. Be assertive, name the specific thing they are doing, and say that it is inappropriate. Often the individual does not realize their actions are being received as harassment.
    2. Make use of resourcesReview our harassment prevention policy, the training material and the relevant legislation, held on the company Dropbox and at every worksite. You can ask the HSE Manager, HR Manager, your supervisor, the President, or any member of the Joint Health and Safety Committee for guidance. You can also contact the OHS Contact Centre to speak with a counsellor about your legal rights, whether or not you choose to file a complaint.
    3. Report itReport any instance of harassment immediately. Your employer must know, or have reason to know, about the harassment to be legally responsible. Tell your supervisor, the HSE or HR Manager, the President, or a member of the Joint Health and Safety Committee. File your report in writing, or follow up a verbal report with a written summary. Keep a copy of anything you submit and anything you receive.
    4. Band together with co-workersIf you are not the only person affected, ask co-workers to write down and report their own incidents. If you are not comfortable doing that, mention when you report that you believe others have been harassed.
    5. Get witnessesIf you can do so safely, talk to people at work who may have witnessed what happened. You may find witnesses, allies, or others who have been harassed by the same person and are willing to support your case.
    6. Gather informationMap out the people and situations that need to be looked at. Give whoever is investigating everything they need to conduct the investigation, based on what you know.
    7. Ask for support from friends and familyHarassment and its aftermath are difficult to go through. Talking with supportive people helps you process what happened, which in turn may help the company investigation or a legal case. You don't need to feel alone.
    If you suspect someone else is being harassed, let them know you support them and encourage them to take these steps. Don't allow anyone to dismiss harassment as harmless or as "just how it is around here". Standing up to workplace harassment is everyone's responsibility.

    Dealing with violence in the workplace

    1. Recognize the warning signs

    • Angry outbursts
    • Intimidating behaviour toward one or more people
    • Talk about weapons, especially if it seems obsessive
    • Blaming others for their own problems
    • Holding grudges

    2. Take it seriously

    Treat all incidents that involve workplace violence or potential workplace violence, including threats, very seriously.

    3. Avoid confrontation

    Do your best to defuse the situation and remove yourself from the area before an incident occurs.

    4. Report it

    You must report work-related violence and threatening behaviour immediately to your supervisor, the HSE or HR Manager, the President, or a member of the Joint Health and Safety Committee, before the situation gets out of hand.

    A client's site rep has twice shouted at your party chief and today mentioned, unprompted, what he keeps in his truck. What is the right next move?

    Correct. Avoid confrontation, get your people out of the area, and report immediately. Third party behaviour is still our responsibility to act on.

    Not quite. Talk about weapons is a recognized warning sign. Avoid confrontation, remove the crew from the area, and report it immediately, third party conduct is still covered.

    Section 6

    What Alberta OHS requires

    You do not need to memorize legislation. You do need to know the protections, duties and reporting expectations that apply to you.

    That includes developing and implementing policies and programs, and providing information and instruction on them, which is what this course is.

    What the OHS Act states

    • Employers must, as far as reasonably practicable, ensure their workers are not subject to or participate in harassment or violence at the work site.
    • Supervisors must, as far as reasonably practicable, ensure workers under their supervision are not subject to harassment or violence at the work site.
    • Workers must refrain from causing or participating in harassment or violence.

    Part 27 of the OHS Code

    Part 27 sets out the technical requirements for violence and harassment prevention in Alberta. It covers the rules an employer must follow for:

    • developing and implementing a violence and harassment prevention plan
    • reviewing that plan, at least every three years, and sooner after an incident or at the request of the health and safety committee
    • involving workers in developing, implementing and reviewing the plan
    • training workers in violence and harassment prevention
    • investigating incidents of violence or harassment
    • supporting a worker affected by violence or harassment at the work site
    Current Alberta requirement. Part 27 now uses one violence and harassment prevention plan. Violence and harassment remain workplace hazards and must be addressed along with other work site hazards. The plan must cover prevention measures, reporting, investigation, confidentiality, worker training and review requirements.

    Beyond OHS law, the Alberta Human Rights Act covers discrimination and harassment based on protected grounds, and the Criminal Code covers assault, threats and criminal harassment. Federally regulated workplaces are also subject to the Canada Labour Code and the Workplace Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations.

    Section 7

    Our commitment at Vista

    The practical message behind both policies is simple: harassment and violence are not part of the job, regardless of who they come from.

    1.4   HARASSMENT POLICY

    At Vista Geomatics Ltd. we are committed to providing a safe and respectful work environment for all staff and customers by mitigating or eliminating the potential for harassment in the workplace. No person has the right to harass another and no person is required or expected to tolerate being the subject of harassment. Vista Geomatics Ltd. has zero tolerance for workplace harassment of any kind and will be proactive in the prevention of workplace violence and harassment.

    The Canadian Human Rights Act and the Canada Labour Code protect us from harassment. The Criminal Code protects us from physical and sexual assault. You have a right to live and work without being harassed, and if you are harassed, you can do something about it. This policy provides information on the steps to take when information regarding harassment has been reported to either a fellow worker, supervisor, or manager.

    Vista Geomatics Ltd. promises to treat all complaints of harassment seriously, whether they are made informally or formally. An investigation will be conducted to act upon and rectify all complaints to ensure that they are resolved quickly, confidentially, and fairly. We will discipline anyone who has harassed a person or group of people. We will discipline managers who do not act properly to end harassment. At Vista Geomatics Ltd. we will not tolerate harassment.

    1.5   WORKPLACE VIOLENCE POLICY

    The management at Vista Geomatics Ltd. recognizes the potential for workplace violence and other aggressive behaviour directed at our employees. We will not tolerate behaviour from anyone that intimidates, threatens, abuses, injures or otherwise victimizes our employees, and will take whatever steps are appropriate to protect our employees from the potential risks associated with workplace violence. Vista Geomatics Ltd. is committed to mitigating or eliminating the potential for workplace violence, thus providing our employees with an appropriate level of protection.

    Vista Geomatics Ltd. employees are required to be familiar with, and follow, the procedures that are in place to protect them from workplace violence. They are also required to immediately report all incidents of workplace violence to their Supervisor or to the HSE Manager. All reported cases of workplace violence will be investigated, and the proper actions will be taken.

    To support workers in establishing and maintaining a workplace which is free from violence, we shall ensure that no employee is penalized, reprimanded or criticized when acting in good faith while following the procedures set forth for addressing situations involving workplace violence.
